paras: The Danville camp meeting riot was a series of attacks by white men on a colored Baptist camp meeting at Danville, about ten miles south of Hillsboro in Highland County, Ohio, in late July 1880. Attackers driven off at night returned in larger numbers on Sunday, broke up the meeting, and reportedly fired on worshippers leaving in wagons. One white attacker, William Dickman, died of a gunshot wound; reported Black deaths were never confirmed. Papers outside Ohio made the attack a point in the 1880 campaign, and the Hillsboro paper answered that Danville was a Democratic township.

The complaint against the attackers was sworn by A. G. Mallory of the Wilmington colored Baptist church, called "the Wilmington preacher" in the local paper. Danville was the voting place of Hamer township, which the Highland Weekly News described as the county's Democratic stronghold.

According to a Cincinnati dispatch of July 26, "a party of drunken roughs" went to the camp at about 10 o'clock at night with pistols, clubs and stones. The dispatch said Friday night, while Mallory's sworn affidavit dated the attack Saturday night, July 24. The attackers were repulsed, and Dickman, one of their number, was shot through the body. Witnesses later testified that fifteen to forty white men faced twelve or thirteen Black men, and all agreed that the whites began the attack and fired first. Jake White, another attacker, was badly beaten, and Frank Manker was shot in the head.

On Sunday afternoon a party "said to number two hundred" attacked again, and the meeting broke up after a desperate fight. The St. Louis Republican, quoted in a Tennessee paper, said this mob carried pistols, shotguns, rifles and carbines. As the worshippers left, women and children in wagons were shot at in Danville, according to the Jackson Standard; the local paper confirmed that a wagon was fired into there. The wire said some colored people were thought killed but scattered too fast for facts to be gathered, and a Minnesota brief said three persons were badly, probably fatally, injured.

Dickman died the following week; Coroner Barrere held an inquest, but its verdict had not been filed when the local paper reported his death. On Mallory's affidavit, sworn July 27, warrants issued against Gus and William Dickman, White, Manker, William Eggling and others for disturbing a religious meeting. In a separate examination, George Charles and William Boelzner were bound over to the Common Pleas Court and two others discharged.

Eggling fled but was arrested late in August at the Sabina Fair and recognized to the Probate Court. After several continuances, Mayor Beeson bound Gus Dickman, White and Manker over to the Probate Court in $300 each. No one had been arrested for firing into the wagon as of early August, and no report of a trial appears in the coverage.

Most papers carried the Cincinnati dispatch, reprinted in Pennsylvania, Michigan and Kansas under headings such as "A Bloody Fight at a Camp Meeting" and "Camp-Meeting Broken Up." It ran among the week's crimes, as did a Mankato brief that dated the breakup "the 25th" and said the roughs first tried to demolish the sutler's tent.

The Jackson Standard ended its item with "Let us send more missionaries to Africa!" The St. Louis Republican, quoted by the Milan Exchange, called it "an outrage upon negroes in the loyal state of Ohio" and said that in the South it would have fed the Republican campaign. The Selma Argus, as quoted in Hillsboro, blamed white Republicans and called it "a story of race prejudice, of outrage, of crime, of murder."

The Republican Highland Weekly News headed its reports "Danville's Disgrace" and "The Danville Rioters" and followed the hearings into September. It answered the Argus with election returns showing Danville Democratic, noting that arrests had been made and one attacker had died. All of the coverage came from white papers; no Black-press account appears in it.

The wire dated the night attack Friday, the sworn affidavit Saturday, July 24, and the Hillsboro paper used both days. Black casualties appear only in general terms, from the dispatch's unconfirmed deaths to the Argus's "dozen or more" seriously wounded; local reports name none.

bases: Armed white men twice attacked a Black Baptist camp meeting and fired on worshippers leaving through Danville, aiming at the gathering rather than any named person (A1, A4, A12).

The Cincinnati wire dispatch (A1), the Jackson Standard (A4), the St. Louis Republican as quoted (A6) and the Hillsboro paper's court reports (A3, A10, A12) independently agree that white men attacked the camp meeting and broke it up.

accounts.label: Cincinnati wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Drunken roughs attacked on Friday night and were repulsed, Dickman being shot; about 200 attacked Sunday and broke up the meeting; some colored people thought killed; no arrests.

accounts.label: St. Louis Republican (quoted)
accounts.gist: A mob of about 200 armed with pistols, shotguns, rifles and carbines drove off the worshippers and fired into wagon-loads of them; some said killed, many wounded.

accounts.label: Selma Argus (quoted)
accounts.gist: White Republicans attacked on two nights, wounding a dozen or more, and fired on the fleeing people in Danville's streets the next day; no arrests reported.

accounts.label: Hillsboro paper and hearing testimony
accounts.gist: Fifteen to forty whites attacked twelve or thirteen Black men on Saturday night, July 24; the whites began it and fired first; a wagon was fired into in Danville on Sunday; several attackers were arrested and bound over.

framing.detail: The Cincinnati dispatch ran as 'A Bloody Fight at a Camp Meeting' and 'Camp-Meeting Broken Up', calling the attackers 'drunken roughs'.
The Jackson Standard closed its item with the sarcastic 'Let us send more missionaries to Africa!'
The St. Louis Republican called it 'an outrage upon negroes in the loyal state of Ohio' while using it to score against Northern Republicans.

The Republican Highland Weekly News headlined 'Danville's Disgrace' and 'disgraceful camp meeting riot', hoped the attackers would be punished, and rebutted the Selma Argus's charge that Ohio Republicans were responsible.

conflicts.note: The sworn affidavit read at the hearing gives Saturday, July 24, and the local paper uses Saturday in most items; the wire dispatch says Friday. The affidavit is the better evidence.
